author: Bella Caracta
title: Former USPS employee, association director unsurprised by federal raid on distribution center - NewsBreak
text:
By Bella Caracta ,
3 hours ago
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Tia Yates feels like she's been screaming from the rooftops about issues inside U.S. Postal Service.
"I've contacted everybody," she said. "Nothing ever happens."
Kansas City council approves financing plan for downtown Royals stadium development Yates worked at the Kansas City, Missouri distribution center for 11 years. She was what you'd call a "career" U.S. Postal Service employee.
"It's heartbreaking because the job is a great job and it's fun," said Yates.
She said one of the reasons Postal Service customers are seeing their packages bounce around the metro is the same reason she no longer works there after more than a decade.
"It's a management problem," she said. "I've literally been one of the people who have actually done the count in the yard and saw that there were trailers full of mail that had already been processed but had been sitting there because management forgot that it was on the lot."
She said it's so disorganized inside the Kansas City, Missouri distribution center that at one point, she could barely walk because of how overloaded with packages it was.
"The mail would constantly pile up. So when (management) would see this mail, they will send us to a different unit," said Yates.
Kansas City real estate company looking into acquiring former Mission Mall site Yates said another explanation for the decline in the Postal Service is changes in hiring practices that are letting bad actors get their hands on customers' valuables.
"When I first started, you had to take a test. You had to take a memory test. You had to take a drug test. None of that happens anymore. They just hire anybody off the street," said Yates.
Frank Albergo, executive director of the Postal Police Officers Association, was not surprised by recent news of a raid by federal agents at the Kansas City distribution center last month.
The Sept. 9 operation was led by the USPS Office of Inspector General and described by a special agent as a "targeted initiative" aimed at "suppressing criminal activity." The USPS OIG said it made several arrests and recovered a stolen firearm.
"It's a major problem. Mail theft has absolutely exploded," said Albergo. "These surges or these raids are great, but they're not going to stop the mail theft problem."
"The Postal Service de-policed itself during a postal crime wave. I mean, that's insane, but that's what they did," said Albergo.
Nationwide, the Postal Police Force has been reduced to a fraction of what it was. According to Albergo, in the 1970s, there were about 2,650 postal police officers. Now there are fewer than 400. Albergo said the Postal Police Force doesn't operate in Kansas City and hasn't for years. He believes reestablishing the Postal Police would help with mail security.

"Need to clean house when it comes to management," said Yates.
